title: Frege versus Extended Frege
formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.
why: This asks whether naming and reusing intermediate formulas can shorten rigorous propositional proofs by more than every polynomial factor. It is a central comparison between strong proof systems and between reasoning with formula trees and shared circuit representations. A separation would yield superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege; an equivalence would show that the extension rule changes shortest-proof lengths by at most polynomial factors.

importance.reason: A canonical strong-system simulation problem, directly tied to Frege lower bounds, finite consistency and circuit-based reasoning.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow formalize Frege rules, fresh extension definitions and polynomial robustness of standard presentations. Their size accounting distinguishes total proof length from the number of lines.

Buss characterizes Frege size simulation of EF through polynomial-size partial EF consistency proofs in Frege, and proves polynomial-size partial Frege self-consistency proofs. The 2002 date on the downloadable typescript is not a new publication.
The Stanford mini-tutorial explicitly presents Frege versus Extended Frege as an open comparison between strong propositional systems.
Aisenberg and coauthors establish polynomial EF and quasipolynomial Frege upper bounds for the Kneser–Lovász principles for each fixed \(k\); no lower-bound separation follows.

Krajíček states a polynomial-size local circuit-rewriting characterization of EF reasoning. The intermediate representations remain circuits; the concluding discussion does not assert a polynomial-time construction by the displayed argument.

ECCC TR26-166, submitted 4 September and published 5 September, reports quasipolynomial Frege simulation of two-group partially commutative formula IPS over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), under its explicit placeholder and axiom conventions.

status_note: Explicitly open in the 2014 source. Bounded primary-source checks through 15 September 2026 did not identify a polynomial-size Frege simulation of unrestricted EF or a superpolynomial separation. The checked June circuit-rewriting and September restricted formula-IPS results have different representations or overhead. The oldest consistency characterization was verified at the author/publisher abstract level in this pass because full-PDF retrieval failed. This individual model and source review is not an exhaustive certification of current openness or an independent verification of new proofs.

context_blocks.text: Frege proofs model a finite list of ordinary propositional deductions. Extended Frege adds named definitions, allowing a long expression to be referenced by a variable after paying for its definition. Chains of these definitions describe shared Boolean circuits. Every assignment to the ordinary variables extends uniquely through an acyclic sequence of definitions, so the extension rule preserves truth of conclusions that contain no extension variables. This explains the systems' common set of theorems while leaving their proof lengths potentially different.

Proof reuse and subformula sharing are different resources. Both systems may cite an earlier proof line many times; ordinary Frege still pays for every occurrence inside each newly written formula. Extended Frege also has names for intermediate expressions. This representational distinction does not itself show that any tautology lacks a short Frege proof. The question compares the best proofs available in the two systems, irrespective of how those proofs were discovered.

The usual robustness theorem compares finite sound and complete Frege presentations with polynomial overhead. Cook and Reckhow also define fresh extension variables and establish the analogous robustness of Extended Frege. The card preserves the saved size-simulation target while making its syntax and bit accounting explicit. It restores the source convention allowing auxiliary ordinary variables; restricting such variables to those of the conclusion gives a polynomially equivalent convention. A bounded-depth, tree-like or otherwise restricted Frege system would be a different question.

A polynomial bound on the existence of translated proofs is distinct from a polynomial-time translator. Buss's work separates these notions and relates size simulation to short finite consistency proofs. His 1991 result characterizes Frege simulation of Extended Frege by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the corresponding partial EF consistency statements: finite propositional assertions that a contradiction has no proof up to a specified length. Frege already has polynomial-size partial self-consistency proofs. This comparison is a stated theorem about the systems, not a resolution of Frege versus EF. The current review checked the author and publisher abstracts; the author's downloadable copy is headed 11 July 2002, although the journal publication is from 1991.

Buss's Stanford tutorial of 27 February 2014 explicitly presents the formula-versus-circuit proof comparison as a longstanding open question. Its discussion of proposed separating principles is historical context, not a current lower-bound theorem. Quasipolynomial upper bounds for particular families must remain distinct both from polynomial upper bounds and from a separation of the unrestricted systems.

A concrete example is the Kneser–Lovász coloring principle. The graph has the \(k\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) as vertices and joins disjoint subsets; for \(n\ge2k\), its propositional principle rules out a proper coloring with \(n-2k+1\) colors. Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs for each fixed \(k\). Constants and exponents may depend on that fixed parameter. Their 2015 conference version states these as Theorems 4 and 5; the 2018 expanded journal abstract retains the fixed-parameter condition. These are upper bounds for particular tautologies, not a superpolynomial Frege lower bound or a uniform bound with both parameters growing.

Krajíček's 11 June 2026 preprint describes circuit-equivalence reasoning by local circuit rewrites. Its relation is polynomial-time recognizable, and each rewrite may delete gates and add at most seven; a short EF proof yields a polynomially bounded chain. The intermediate objects retain circuit sharing. The concluding discussion also distinguishes existence of a small chain from a polynomial-time construction of it by the presented proof. This normal-form statement therefore supplies neither the polynomial-size formula proof nor the polynomial-time translator that could be mistakenly inferred from the abstract.

The September 2026 report by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay states a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a restricted Ideal Proof System over \(\mathrm{GF}(2)\), the field with two elements. Certificates are algebraic formulas. The original variables are divided into two groups, noncommuting within a group and commuting across groups; Definition 1.1 separately specifies the noncommuting placeholder variables and included Boolean and commutator axioms. Theorem 1.2 concerns refutations of unsatisfiable CNFs in that model. Its certificate restrictions and quasipolynomial overhead both prevent it from answering the unrestricted EF question. The report and theorem scope were checked; its complete new proof was not independently verified.

An EF proof includes its final formula, so a superpolynomial separation from Frege would imply superpolynomial Frege proof-size lower bounds as a function of formula length. The converse need not follow: a family hard for Frege might also require long EF proofs. Likewise, the separate question whether EF is polynomially bounded asks whether every tautology has a short EF proof, rather than whether Frege can match EF's shortest proofs. The present card makes no assumption that \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\) and does not identify a computation-class separation with this proof-system comparison.
